q: Your agent compacts history by summarizing it, but after compaction it forgets which files it changed and which errors it already fixed. What should you change?

options.text: Compact more often so each summary covers fewer turns
Tell the summarizer to keep file paths, decisions and errors
Stop compacting and use a model with a larger window
Clear the context after each step instead of compacting

explain: The summarizer prompt decides what survives compaction. Specify what to preserve, such as every file path modified, decisions made, errors and their fixes. An under-specified summarizer is a common multi-session failure.

q: You finished a feature in a long Claude Code session. Your next task is unrelated. What should you do with the context?

options.text: Compact it, so the old feature is summarized for later
Clear it, keeping lasting rules in CLAUDE.md
Keep going; the window will drop the oldest turns
Prune the last few turns and continue in the session

explain: Clearing fits when the next task is completely different; anything that must persist belongs in CLAUDE.md. Compaction suits continuing the same feature near the ceiling, and the window never drops turns on its own.

q: Claude spent ten turns chasing a dead-end debugging theory, and the context is now full of irrelevant output. Which strategy fits?

options.text: Pruning: rewind to before the dead end and drop what followed
Compaction: summarize everything, dead end included
A subagent: hand the same theory to a fresh context
Caching: mark the dead-end turns so they cost less

explain: Pruning rewinds to an earlier message and drops what came after, which suits an unproductive path or debug clutter. Compaction would keep a summary of the clutter.

q: An extraction prompt gets the task right, but the model invents its own nesting and field layout for the output. Which technique is missing?

options.text: A longer description of the task's purpose
Few-shot examples that show the exact structure
A higher effort setting for the extraction step
A system prompt describing the assistant's tone

explain: "Task right, structure invented" maps to few-shot examples: show the exact shape rather than describe it. Diagnose the failure type first, then add the one matching technique.

q: A signature-parsing prompt works on every test email but breaks on emails with two signatures. What should you add?

options.text: A constraint or example covering the two-signature case
A rewrite of the whole prompt in a more formal style
A larger model for every email, to handle variety
A line asking the model to read each email carefully

explain: Clean on tested inputs but breaking on a variant means the prompt lacks a constraint or example for that variant. Add exactly that, re-run, and diagnose again if it still fails.

q: Over five revisions a prompt kept growing. Outputs now run over 2,000 characters per call and latency rose, with no gain in accuracy. What does the course say is happening?

options.text: Long prompts trigger a slower, more careful model mode
The model calibrates length to the input; trim to what matters
The prompt is too short; add more detail so answers tighten
Long prompts lower the temperature, so output gets wordier

explain: A verbose prompt produces verbose output: more latency, no accuracy gain. Keep the constraints that change behavior and remove the rest. A prompt that grows every pass is a sign of skipped diagnosis.

q: In an agentic loop, Claude sometimes passes malformed arguments to a tool, and your code crashes. Which setting constrains the tool arguments?

options.text: `strict: true` on the tool definition
`output_config.format` with `json_schema`
A prefilled `{` at the start of the reply
`disable_parallel_tool_use` on the request

explain: Strict tool use validates tool arguments against the input schema before your code runs. `output_config.format` constrains the final response text, not tool arguments, and you can use both in one request.

q: You enabled JSON outputs with a schema. Which two cases must your code still handle? (Choose two.)

options.text: `stop_reason: refusal`, with no usable JSON in the reply
`stop_reason: max_tokens`, with the JSON cut off midway
Tokens that break the schema appearing mid-response
A prefill needed to start the JSON object correctly
Field names drifting away from the schema over time

explain: Constrained decoding stops schema-breaking tokens, but success isn't guaranteed: a refusal or hitting `max_tokens` leaves no parseable result. Check `stop_reason` before parsing. JSON outputs can't be combined with prefilling.

q: An agent worked through 50 turns in testing. In production its context fills by turn 8. What does the course point to?

options.text: Production tool outputs are often 3–5× larger than test fixtures
Production traffic uses a smaller context window by default
The API silently drops turns faster under heavy load
Production users write much longer system prompts

explain: Every tool result stays in context, and production tool outputs run 3–5× longer than fixtures. Measure tool-result token cost against the largest real input before shipping.

q: Claude needs to search 200 files to find where a config value is set. The output would flood the main conversation. What fits?

options.text: A subagent that explores in its own context and returns a summary
Pasting all 200 files into the main conversation at once
Compacting the conversation before the search starts
Clearing the context and losing the current task

explain: Subagent handoffs isolate self-contained subtasks, especially exploration, and return only a summary. You lose visibility into intermediate steps but keep the main context clean.

q: A tool-heavy agent session keeps approaching the context ceiling. Which two steps does the course recommend? (Choose two.)

options.text: Prune tool outputs once they have been used
Compact the history before reaching the cap
Rely on the API to truncate the oldest turns
Strip thinking blocks out of earlier turns
Ask Claude to keep its answers much shorter

explain: Prune tool outputs after use and compact before the cap. The API never truncates for you, and thinking blocks must be returned unchanged, so stripping them breaks the request.

q: A ticket classifier should return `BILLING`, `TECHNICAL` or `ESCALATION`, but it replies "This looks like a billing issue." Which technique is missing?

options.text: An output constraint: exactly one label, and nothing else
A longer explanation of what each category means
A higher effort setting so the model is more precise
A friendlier system prompt describing the assistant

explain: Wrong shape, such as a sentence instead of a label, means a missing output constraint: the allowed values, the form and where to stop. For example: "Exactly one of: BILLING, TECHNICAL, ESCALATION. Return only the label."

q: You diagnosed a failure and added the one matching technique. What comes next in the course's prompt-fixing loop?

options.text: Re-run, and diagnose again if it still fails
Add two more techniques to be safe
Ship it, since the right fix was applied
Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch

explain: The rule is: name the failure, add the one matching technique, re-run, and diagnose again if it still fails. Adding techniques without diagnosis makes the prompt longer, not more precise.

q: A parser feeds a strict downstream contract, and its edge cases can be covered by tests. Which four techniques does the course stack for a reliable output shape in this situation?

options.text: System prompt, XML tags, few-shot examples and output constraints
Temperature 0, higher effort, retries and a longer prompt
Prefilling, extended thinking, caching and batch processing
A larger model, more tools, subagents and a bigger window

explain: The four techniques for a reliable output shape are a system prompt, XML tags, few-shot examples and output constraints. Stack all four for a clearly defined output contract with coverable edge cases; for a simple task, simplify instead.

q: The first request with a new JSON schema is noticeably slower, but later requests with the same schema are fast. Why?

options.text: The schema is compiled to a grammar once, then cached
The model warms up after its first structured reply
The first response is always routed to a slower model
The SDK downloads the schema on the first request

explain: With structured outputs, a new schema is compiled into a grammar on first use, and compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use. That first-call latency is one of the costs.

q: After enabling JSON outputs, your input token count per request rose slightly. Why?

options.text: The API adds a format-describing system prompt
The schema is sent back inside every response
JSON outputs turn on extended thinking
The response is generated twice and compared

explain: Structured outputs inject a system prompt describing the format, billed as normal input tokens. Constrained decoding then keeps the output valid against the schema.

q: Your code prefills the assistant reply with `{` and also sets `output_config.format` to a JSON schema. What does the course say about this combination?

options.text: They are incompatible; pick the one that fits the task
It is the recommended way to force valid JSON output
Prefill is required for JSON outputs to work at all
It works, but only with streaming turned on

explain: JSON outputs and prefilling the assistant message are incompatible, so pick the one that fits the task. With JSON outputs, constrained decoding already enforces the schema at generation time.

q: A date extractor returns valid JSON that passes every schema check, but for sentences mentioning two dates it often picks the wrong one. What does this show?

options.text: Validation checks shape, not whether the value is right
The schema is broken and must be rewritten
Structured outputs don't work for date fields
The model needs a higher temperature for dates

explain: Schema validation confirms shape, not correctness. Add graded eval cases for edge inputs such as two dates, no date or "next Tuesday", then fix the prompt; the eval detects the problem and the prompt changes the output.
